prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands at the left-right mirror of the chosen anchor: a brick dx cells wide chosen at column x lands at column 8 - dx - x, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no results yet. The starting network learned to press DONE at once on every design (100% of episodes). Random placements earn negative reward, so stopping early is the safe local optimum. The likely cause is the mirror rule: a brick placed at anchor column x lands at column 8-dx-x. The starting network scores each anchor from local conv features at that same cell, so it cannot see the cells the brick will actually fill. It never finds positive-reward actions and gives up. Fixing this mismatch in the action head should matter more than any other change. I test two remedies. (1) Concatenate the column-flipped trunk features after a learned layer, so pooling over the anchor's footprint covers the real landing cells. (2) A learned per-channel mixing across columns, which can learn any column remapping, not only the mirror. A third candidate repeats (1) with fewer PPO epochs, which buys more training samples, plus higher entropy to resist the early-DONE collapse.

### Round 2
Mirroring the features before the footprint-pooling head fixed the early-DONE collapse. That model scored 0.53 with the default recipe. A learned column-mixing layer reached only 0.40, so building the mirror into the network beats learning it within this budget. The best so far, r1c3, uses the same network with 2 PPO epochs and entropy 0.02. It scored 0.725, and both seeds agreed (0.727 and 0.723). That suggests more samples, meaning more fresh designs, helps a lot, and its training success was still rising at the end (0.38 at 75%, 0.65 at 100%). Dev IoU is 0.966 with about 0.8 wrong cells per episode, so most failures are small precision errors, not wrong strategy. Next steps: push the sample count further with 1 epoch; give more credit to the final +1 exact-build bonus with higher gamma and lambda; and test whether a larger head, fed only the mirrored features, fixes precision errors when checking where a brick lands.

### Round 3
The key fix was mirroring the trunk features before the per-footprint pooling head (flip-concat, r1c1, 0.53). Changing to 2 PPO epochs with entropy 0.02 (r1c3) raised this to 0.725, and both seeds agreed (0.73 and 0.72). Training success was still rising at the end of r1c3's run, so this budget seems to limit learning by samples and optimisation speed, not network capacity. One epoch (r2c1) gave a full early-DONE collapse in both seeds, so learning needs enough optimisation per sample. Gamma 0.99 (r2c2, 0.30) and the larger mirrored-only head (r2c3, 0.48) both did worse and varied a lot between seeds. The traces show the remaining errors: the agent places bricks in the wrong order around overhangs, for example dropping a 1x1 where a 1x2 overhang should go, after which the target cannot be completed. The ideas left to test are faster learning (a higher learning rate), giving the placement scores global context, and a larger receptive field for planning how the target splits into bricks.

### Round 4
Mirroring the trunk features (flip-concat) and pooling them over each brick footprint is what lets the agent learn this world at all. Without it, or with a learned column remap (0.40), results are much weaker. The recipe matters a lot. Two PPO epochs gave 0.72, against 0.53 with four. One epoch collapsed into ending every episode with DONE straight away (0.00). Raising lr to 0.002 gave the best result, 0.89, with both seeds close together. A larger network costs samples and lost: a deeper trunk scored 0.56 and a wider head 0.48. A longer gamma made seeds unstable (0.30). The global-context head (0.76 vs 0.72) is within noise. r3c1's training curve was still rising at the end (0.72 to 0.83), so the agent is still limited by optimisation speed at this budget. In this final round I keep the r3c1 network and push optimisation speed: lr 0.003, more minibatch steps per update, and the global-context head combined with lr 0.002.

## Trial it ended with
name: r3c1 with 32 minibatches
hypothesis: Same as r3c1, but n_minibatches is 32 instead of 16. This doubles the gradient steps per update (64 instead of 32) with smaller minibatches, at the same sample budget and compute. Training is limited by optimisation speed, so more steps per batch should help, as the higher lr did. Refuted if dev success is at most about 0.85.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

That gives what changes (the landing column) and exactly how (a left-right mirror, 8-dx-x), which matches the hidden rule. Later rounds keep building on it, for example Round 4: "Mirroring the trunk features (flip-concat)... is what lets the agent learn this world at all."
